title: Shigetaka Kurita's 176 emoji
hook: The emoji that won the world began as 176 pictures, each 12 pixels square.
peek: In 1999 a Japanese phone company asked a young designer for little pictures that could fit in a text message. Shigetaka Kurita drew 176 of them on a tiny grid, and today the originals belong to the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
lede: In 1999 the Japanese mobile operator NTT Docomo launched i-mode, an early way to use the internet on a phone. Screens were tiny and messages short, so Shigetaka Kurita, on the i-mode team, designed a set of 176 symbols to help say more with less. Each one fit on a grid just 12 pixels wide and 12 pixels tall.

bullets.text: Kurita drew on the symbols of weather forecasts, road signs and the visual shorthand of manga, such as a light bulb for an idea. He wanted pictures that worked at a glance on a small screen.
Kurita's set is the most famous early one, but not the very first. The rival operator J-Phone had put about 90 symbols on one of its phones in 1997. Docomo's set is the one that spread.
The word sounds like "emotion" but comes from Japanese: e means picture and moji means character. The resemblance is a coincidence that probably helped the word catch on in English.

In 2016 the Museum of Modern Art added Kurita's original 176 emoji to its collection, alongside other digital designs. The set was a gift from NTT Docomo, the company that first asked Kurita to draw it.
